nodes.name: Transient improvement of CMRAC remains a conjecture
nodes.statement: While the results of these papers established stability of combined schemes, no rigorous guarantees of improved transient performance were provided, and have remained a conjecture \cite{eugeneTAC09}.
nodes.statement_short: Whether combined direct/indirect adaptive control (CMRAC) provably improves transients was left open.

nodes.name: Linear plant dynamics with scalar input
nodes.statement: \be \dot x(t) = A_p x(t) + b u(t) \ee where ${x(t) \in \Re^n}$ is the state vector, ${u(t)\in \Re}$ is the control input, ${A_p\in \Re^{n \times n}}$ is unknown and ${b\in \Re^n}$ is known.
nodes.statement_short: Unknown-$A_p$ linear plant with known input vector $b$ and scalar control $u$.

nodes.name: Closed--loop reference model (CRM)
nodes.statement: \be \dot x_m(t) = A_m x_m(t) + b r(t) - L(x(t)-x_m(t)) \ee where ${A_m \in \Re^{n\times n }}$ is Hurwtitz and ${r(t)\in \Re}$ is a bounded possible time varying reference command. ${L\in \Re^{n\times n}}$ is denoted as the {\em Luenberger--gain}, and is chosen such that
nodes.statement_short: Reference model fed back through the Luenberger gain $L$ on the model-following error.

nodes.name: Hurwitz CRM system matrix $\bar A_m$
nodes.statement: \be \bar A_m \triangleq A_m+L \ee is Hurwitz. Equation \eqref{s1:ref} is referred to as a CRM, and when ${L=0}$ the classical ORM is recovered.
nodes.statement_short: $\bar A_m=A_m+L$ must be Hurwitz; $L=0$ recovers the classical ORM.

nodes.name: Adaptive control input
nodes.statement: \be u(t)= \theta^T(t) x(t) + r(t) \ee where $\theta(t) \in \Re^n$ is the adaptive control gain with the update law

nodes.name: Adaptive update law
nodes.statement: \be \dot \theta(t) = -\Gamma x(t)e^T(t) Pb \ee with ${\Gamma = \Gamma^T>0}$, ${e(t)= x(t)-x_m(t)}$ is the model following error and $P=P^T>0$ is the solution to the algebraic Lyapunov equation
nodes.statement_short: Gradient-type tuning law driven by $x e^T P b$ with gain $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Algebraic Lyapunov equation
nodes.statement: \be \bar A_m^TP+P \bar A_m = -I_{n\times n}. \ee

nodes.name: CRM error model
nodes.statement: The underlying error model in this case is given by \be\dot e(t)= \bar A_m e(t) + b \tilde\theta(t)x(t) \ee where ${\tilde\theta(t)=\theta(t)-\theta^*}$ is the parameter error.
nodes.statement_short: Model-following error obeys $\dot e=\bar A_m e+b\tilde\theta x$ with $\tilde\theta=\theta-\theta^*$.

nodes.name: Assumption 1: matching condition
nodes.statement: A parameter vector ${\theta^*\in\Re^n}$ exists that satisfies the {\em matching condition} \be A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: A constant $\theta^*$ exists with $A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1: global stability of the CRM--adaptive system
nodes.statement: The closed-loop adaptive system with \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u} and \eqref{s1:law} is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically, under the matching condition in \eqref{s1:match}.
nodes.statement_short: The CRM--adaptive system is globally stable and its model-following error vanishes asymptotically.
assumptions: The closed-loop adaptive system with \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u} and \eqref{s1:law}
under the matching condition in \eqref{s1:match}
conclusions: is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically

nodes.name: Lyapunov candidate $V(e,\tilde\theta)$
nodes.statement: \be V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta \ee
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic Lyapunov candidate in the tracking error and the parameter error.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: It is straight forward to show using \eqref{s1:law} and \eqref{s1:et} that \be V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta \ee is a Lyapunov function. Since $e$ is bounded, the structure of \eqref{s1:ref} implies that $x_m$ is bounded. $x$ in turn and $u$ are bounded. Barbalat lemma ensures asymptotic convergence of $e(t)$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit the Lyapunov function $V=e^TPe+\tilde\theta^T\Gamma^{-1}\tilde\theta$, chain boundedness, then apply Barbalat's lemma.

nodes.name: Lyapunov function
nodes.statement: It is straight forward to show using \eqref{s1:law} and \eqref{s1:et} that \be V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta \ee is a Lyapunov function.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the quadratic form is a Lyapunov function for the error dynamics.

nodes.name: Boundedness chain
nodes.statement: Since $e$ is bounded, the structure of \eqref{s1:ref} implies that $x_m$ is bounded. $x$ in turn and $u$ are bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Propagate boundedness of $e$ to $x_m$, $x$ and $u$.

nodes.name: Barbalat conclusion
nodes.statement: Barbalat lemma ensures asymptotic convergence of $e(t)$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $e(t)\to 0$ by Barbalat's lemma.

nodes.name: Corollary 2: finite time $T(\epsilon,L)$ for error smallness
nodes.statement: For all $\epsilon>0$ there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norm{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$.
assumptions: For all $\epsilon>0$
conclusions: there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norm{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$

nodes.name: Open--loop reference model and true tracking error
nodes.statement: \be\dot x_m^o(t) = A_m x_m^o(t) + b r(t) \ee with the corresponding tracking error \be e^o(t) = x(t) - x_m^o(t) . \ee
nodes.statement_short: The classical ORM $\dot x_m^o=A_mx_m^o+br$ and the true tracking error $e^o=x-x_m^o$.

nodes.name: Corollary 3: $x(t)$ converges to the open--loop reference state
nodes.statement: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
assumptions: The overall CRM--adaptive system is defined by \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u}, and \eqref{s1:law}.
conclusions: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm:simple} we can conclude that $e(t)\rightarrow0$ asymptotically. Thus we can conclude that $x_m(t) \rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $e(t)\rightarrow 0$, implying that $e^o\rightarrow 0$, thus $x(t)\rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain $e\to0\Rightarrow x_m\to x_m^o\Rightarrow e^o\to0$.

nodes.name: Remark on the nonlinear character of the CRM
nodes.statement: The choice of the CRM as in (2) essentially makes the reference model nonlinear, as $x$ depends on $\theta$ which in turn depends on $x_m$ in a highly nonlinear manner. In general, the tracking problem in a ORM--adaptive system can be viewed as one where an overall nonlinear time-varying system is to be designed such that its output tracks that of a linear time-invariant system. The CRM-adaptive system is one where the overall nonlinear system is instead required to follow a nonlinear (reference) model. This nonlinear model, however, is chosen such that it asymptotically approaches the original linear reference model in the classical case, and hence the CRM-adaptive system retains all the desired characteristics of the ORM-adaptive system. As we will show in Section \ref{section:perf}, the CRM-adaptive system has an additional desirable property, of quantifiable transient properties, which the ORM-adaptive system may not necessarily possess. We will also show in this section that this is made possible by virtue of the additional degree of freedom available to the adaptive system in the form of the feedback gain in the CRM.
nodes.statement_short: The CRM is a nonlinear reference model that asymptotically approaches the classical linear one, buying quantifiable transients.

nodes.name: Spectral constants $\sigma$, $s$, $a$ and the choices of $L$ and $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Given a Hurwtiz matrix $A_m\in \Re^{n\times n}$ \be \begin{split} \sigma& \triangleq - \max_i \left( \text{real} (\lambda_i(A_m)) \right) \\ s& \triangleq - \min_i \left( \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right)/2 \right) \\ a& \triangleq \norm{A_m}. \end{split} \ee For ease of exposition, throughout the paper, we choose $L$ in \eqref{s1:ref} and $\Gamma$ in \eqref{s2:adaplaw} as follows: \begin{align} L &\triangleq -\ell I_{n \times n} \\ \Gamma & \triangleq \gamma I_{n\times n}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\sigma$, $s$, $a$ from the spectrum and norm of $A_m$, and fixes $L=-\ell I$, $\Gamma=\gamma I$.

nodes.name: Lemma 4: $s\geq\sigma>0$
nodes.statement: The constants $\sigma$ and $s$ are strictly positive and satisfy \ben s\geq\sigma>0. \een
assumptions: Given a Hurwtiz matrix $A_m\in \Re^{n\times n}$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: $A_m$ is Hurwitz and therefore $\sigma>0$. It is not necessary however that the sum $A_m+A_m^T$ is Hurwitz. The trace operator is denoted as $\text{Tr} (\cdot)$ and is a linear operator. Recalling that a matrix and its transpose have the same trace we can conclude that $\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m) =\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m+A_m^T)/2$. Finally we have that \ben s \geq -\frac 1 {2n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right) = -\frac 1 n \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(A_m) \geq \sigma>0. \ \IEEEQED \een
nodes.statement_short: Compare eigenvalue sums of $A_m$ and its symmetric part via the trace, then bound the minimum.

nodes.name: Positivity of sigma
nodes.statement: $A_m$ is Hurwitz and therefore $\sigma>0$.
nodes.statement_short: $A_m$ Hurwitz gives $\sigma>0$.

nodes.name: Trace identity
nodes.statement: It is not necessary however that the sum $A_m+A_m^T$ is Hurwitz. The trace operator is denoted as $\text{Tr} (\cdot)$ and is a linear operator. Recalling that a matrix and its transpose have the same trace we can conclude that $\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m) =\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m+A_m^T)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal traces give equal eigenvalue sums for $A_m$ and its symmetric part.

nodes.name: Conclude the inequality
nodes.statement: Finally we have that \ben s \geq -\frac 1 {2n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right) = -\frac 1 n \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(A_m) \geq \sigma>0. \ \IEEEQED \een
nodes.statement_short: Average the eigenvalues to obtain $s\geq\sigma>0$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5: bounds on the Lyapunov matrix $P$
nodes.statement: With $L$ chosen as in \eqref{s1:L}, $A_m$ Hurwitz with constants $\sigma$ and $a$ as defined in \eqref{s1:ambound}, $P$ in \eqref{s1:lyap} satisfies \begin{align} \text{(i)} & &\norm P \leq& \frac{m^2}{\sigma + 2\ell} & &\\ \text{(ii)} & &\min_i \lambda_i{(P)} \geq &\frac{1}{2(s+\ell)}& & \end{align} where $m=(1+4\varkappa)^{n-1} \text{ and } \varkappa \triangleq \frac a \sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: $\norm P\le m^2/(\sigma+2\ell)$ and $\min_i\lambda_i(P)\ge 1/(2(s+\ell))$.
assumptions: With $L$ chosen as in \eqref{s1:L}, $A_m$ Hurwitz with constants $\sigma$ and $a$ as defined in \eqref{s1:ambound}

nodes.name: Assumption 2: known bound on $\theta^*$
nodes.statement: A known $\theta^*_{max}$ exists such that $\norm{\theta^*}\leq \theta^*_{max}$.

nodes.name: Projection-based adaptive law and the convex function $f$
nodes.statement: The projection based adaptive law, which replaces \eqref{s1:law}, is given by \be \dot \theta(t) = \text{Proj}_\Gamma \left(\theta(t),-x e^T P b ,f \right) \ee where the $\Gamma$--projection function, $\text{Proj}_\Gamma$, is defined as in Appendix \ref{ap:proj} and $f$ is a convex function given by \be f(\theta;\vartheta,\varepsilon) = \frac{\norm \theta^2 -\vartheta^2}{2 \varepsilon \vartheta - \varepsilon^2} \ee where $\vartheta$ and $\varepsilon$ are positive constants chosen as $\vartheta = \theta^*_\text{max}$ and $\varepsilon>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Replaces the plain tuning law by a $\Gamma$--projection onto the convex set $\{f\le0\}$.

nodes.name: Parameter bounds $\theta_\text{max}$ and $\tilde\theta_\text{max}$
nodes.statement: Using the design parameters of the convex function $f(\theta;\vartheta,\varepsilon)$ we introduce the following definitions \be\begin{split} \theta_\text{max}&\triangleq \vartheta+\varepsilon \text{ and }\\ \tilde\theta_\text{max} &\triangleq 2\vartheta+\varepsilon. \end{split}\ee

Recall that $\tau_1$ is the time scale associated with $e(t)$ and $a_\theta$ is an upper bound on the uncertain open--loop eigen values of the plant. When $\ell\geq \ell^*$ we are able to show that at $t_N=N\tau_1$, $e(t_N)$ has exponentially decade by $N$ time constants, while $x(t_N)$ has not deviated far from $x(0)$.

nodes.statement: The bound on $\dot r(t)$ is needed so that $\dot u(t)$ is well defined. The analysis techniques that follow in proving Theorem \ref{thmudot} will still hold for reference inputs with discontinuities. The metric for transient performance however would change from $\dot u$ to $\frac{d}{dt} \left(\theta^T(t)x(t)\right)$.

nodes.name: Simplified interval bounds on $\sup\abs{\dot u(t)}$
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thmudot}, it follows that \be\begin{split} \sup_{t\in\mathbb T_1}\abs{\dot u(t)} \leq & c_1\rho + c_2 \sqrt\rho + r_1\\ \sup_{t\in\mathbb T_2}\abs{\dot{u}(t)} \leq & \sqrt \rho c_3 + (1+c_{4} l) c_5 + \sqrt{\frac 1 \rho} (1+c_{4} \ell)^2 c_6 \\ &+ \epsilon_1 \mathfrak{L}_1 (\rho,\ell,\sqrt \rho, \ell\sqrt\rho, \ell^2) + r_1\\ \sup_{t\in\mathbb T_3}\abs{\dot{u}(t)} \leq & \sqrt{\frac 1 \rho} (1+c_4\ell )c_7 +c_8\\ &+\epsilon \mathfrak{L}_2 (\rho,\ell,\sqrt \rho, \ell\sqrt\rho, \ell^2,\epsilon_1) + r_1 \end{split} \ee where $c_i>0$, $i=1$ to $8$ are independent of $\ell$ and $\rho$, $\mathfrak L_1(\cdot)$ and $\mathfrak L_2(\cdot)$ are globally lipschitz with respect to their arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Collapses the Theorem 11 bounds into monomials in $\rho,\sqrt\rho,\ell$ on each interval.

nodes.name: Observations (A1)--(A4) on the CRM bounds for $\dot u$
nodes.statement: The inequalities in \eqref{uox} lead us to the following three main observations (see Figure \ref{fig:udot}) \begin{enumerate}[(\bf {A}1)] \item Over $\mathbb T_1$, $\abs{\dot u(t)}$ is bounded by a linear function of $\rho$ and $\sqrt{\rho}$, \item Over $\mathbb T_2$, $\abs{\dot u(t)}$ is bounded by a linear function of $\sqrt \rho,\ell,\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}},\ell \sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$ and $\ell^2\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}} $ \item Over $\mathbb T_3$, $\abs{\dot u(t)}$ is bounded by a linear function of $\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$ and $\ell \sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$ \item $\tau_1$ decreases with $\ell$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Per-interval growth of the $\dot u$ bound in $\rho$ and $\ell$, and the shrinking of $\tau_1$ with $\ell$.

Over $\mathbb T_2$, $\abs{\dot u(t)}$ is bounded by a linear function of $\sqrt \rho,\ell,\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}},\ell \sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$ and $\ell^2\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}} $
Over $\mathbb T_3$, $\abs{\dot u(t)}$ is bounded by a linear function of $\sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$ and $\ell \sqrt {\frac{1}{\rho}}$

nodes.name: Remark on time-scale separation as the driver of the bounds
nodes.statement: The main idea used for the derivation of the bounds in Theorem \ref{thmudot} is time--scale separation of the error dynamics decay, and the worst case open--loop eigenvalues of the uncertain plant. The most important point to note is that $\tau_1$ can be made small by choosing a large $\ell$. There is a penalty, however, in choosing a large $\ell$, as the bound $G_{x,2}$ increases linearly with $\ell$. Therefore, after choosing an $\ell$ which satisfies the time scale separation as needed in Lemma \ref{tscalesep}, a $\rho$ (which through \eqref{rhos} defines a choice for $\gamma$) can be chosen such that the integral in the following theorem is minimized.

nodes.name: Optimal choice of $(\rho,\ell)$ minimizing the truncated $\mathcal L_2$ norm of $\dot u$
nodes.statement: \be \left(\rho_\text{opt},\ell_\text{opt}\right)=\argmin_{{\rho>0} \atop{\ell\geq\ell^*}} \norm{\dot u(\rho,\ell)}_{L_2, \tau} \ee for any $0 < \tau < T_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\norm{\dot u(\rho,\ell)}_{L_2,\tau}$ over $\rho>0$, $\ell\ge\ell^*$.

nodes.name: Theorem 12: existence of optimal $\rho$ and $\ell$

nodes.statement_short: A minimizer $(\rho_\text{opt},\ell_\text{opt})$ of the truncated $\mathcal L_2$ norm of $\dot u$ exists.
assumptions: for any $0 < \tau < T_1$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12
nodes.statement: $\norm{\dot u(\rho,\ell)}_{L_2, \tau}$ is continuous with respect to $\rho$ and $\ell$ where $\rho$ and $\ell$ appear in the numerator of \eqref{uox} and are positive. Therefore, $\rho_\text{opt}$ and $\ell_\text{opt}$ exist and are finite.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity and positivity of the bound in its arguments give a finite minimizer.

nodes.statement: The bounds in \eqref{uox2} indicate that in the classical ORM, one can only derive a bound for $\dot u$ over the period $\mathbb T_1^\prime$, $\mathbb T_2^\prime$ and $\mathbb T_3^\prime$. nodes.name: Water--bed effect simulation
nodes.statement: The discussions in the preceding sections clearly show that CRM-adaptive systems introduce a trade--off: a fast convergence in $e(t)$ with a reduced $\norml{\dot\theta(t)}{2}$ occurs at the expense of an increased $e^o(t)$. While an optimal choice of $\rho$ and $\ell$ can minimize this trade--off, it also implies that a badly chosen $\ell$ and $\rho$ can significantly worsen the adaptive system performance in terms of $e^o(t)$ and $\dot u(t)$. We denote this as the water--bed effect and illustrate it through a simulation. Consider a first-order plant with a single unknown parameter, whose values are identical to the example in Section \ref{simstud1} over the first ten seconds. Figure \ref{fig:ta1} shows the behavior of $\dot u(t)$ for the ORM, the optimized CRM, and a poorly chosen CRM. The plots clearly show the water--bed effect for the last case and the improved performance of the optimized CRM over the ORM. The free design parameters are also shown in the figure.
nodes.statement_short: A first-order plant showing that badly chosen $\ell,\rho$ trade fast $e$ decay for worse $e^o$ and $\dot u$.

nodes.name: Simulation study: scalar time-varying plant with disturbance
nodes.statement: For this study a scalar time varying system of the form in \eqref{s2:sys} is controlled where \ben A_p(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & 0 \leq t < 20 \\ 1+\frac{1}{4} (t-20) & 20 \leq t <24 \\ 2 & t \geq 24 \end{cases}, \een $b=1$, and $d(t)$ is a deterministic signal used to represent a disturbance. Over the first 20 seconds $d(t)=0$. After 20 seconds $d(t)$ is generated from a Gausian distribution centered at 0 with a variance of 1, covariance of 0.1, deterministically sampled at 10 Hz with a fixed seed, and then passed through a saturation function with upper and lowers bounds of 0.2 and -0.2 respectively. The reference model to be followed is defined as \be \dot x_m = - x_m + r + \ell(x-x_m) \ee with control input from \eqref{s1:u} and the update law for the adaptive parameter defined \eqref{s1:law}, where $\ell$ and $\rho$ are chosen as in Table \ref{t:scen}.
nodes.statement_short: Scalar plant with a ramped parameter and a saturated Gaussian disturbance, comparing ORM and CRM.

nodes.name: Discussion of the CRM simulation results
nodes.statement: The simulations have three distinct regions of interest, with Region 1 denoting the first 10 seconds, Region 2 denoting the 10 sec to 20 sec range, and Region 3 denoting the 20 sec to 35 sec range. In Region 1, the adaptive system is subjected to non--zero initial conditions in the state and the reference input is zero. At $t=10$ sec, the beginning of Region 2, a filtered step input is introduced. At $t=20$ sec In Region 3, time-variations in the plant parameter as well, disturbances and a filtered step input are introduced. Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the response of the CRM--adaptive system over 0 to 35 seconds, with $x_m$, $x$, and $e$ indicated in Figure 2, and $u$, $\dot u$, and $\theta$ indicated in Figure 3. In both cases, the resulting performance is compared with the classical adaptive system. The first point that should be noted is a satisfactory behavior in the steady-state of the CRM--adaptive controller. In particular, as can be seen from the latter half of Region 1, both $e$ and $e^o$ tend to zero as $t$ approaches 10 seconds. The same satisfactory trends are observed in regions 2 and 3 as well, underscoring the robustness property of CRM--adaptive control, which validates Theorem 2. We also note yet another significant difference between the responses of CRM--adaptive control and the classical one, which pertains to the rate of control input $\dot u$. An examination of Regions 2 and 3 clearly illustrates that the control input is smoother for CRM--adaptive control.
nodes.statement_short: Across the three regions the CRM tracks well and yields a visibly smoother control input than the classical scheme.

nodes.name: CMRAC--C identifier and error dynamics
nodes.statement: We assume that the plant and reference model dynamics are given by Equations \eqref{s1:sys} and \eqref{s1:ref} with $A_m$ and $L=L_m$ satisfying Equations \eqref{s1:match} and \eqref{s1:ambar}. For ease of exposition we choose \be L_m=L= -\ell I_{n\times n} \text{ and } L_i=-(\sigma+\ell)I_{n\times n}. \ee

nodes.name: Simulation study: CMRAC--CO under measurement noise
nodes.statement: For this study a scalar system in the presence of noise is to be controlled with dynamics as presented in \eqref{p:n}, where $A_p = 1$, $b=1$, and $n(t)$ is a deterministic signal used to represent sensor noise. $n(t)$ is generated from a Gausian distribution with variance 1 and covariance 0.01, deterministically sampled using a fixed seed at 100 Hz, and then passed through a saturation function with upper and lower bounds of 0.1 and -0.1 respectively. The reference model, identifier and observer are from \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s8:o} and \eqref{s6:o} respectively, with $A_m=-1$ and $b=1$. The controller is defined by \eqref{s6:law}. The design parameters for the two test cases are shown in Table \ref{baus}.
nodes.statement_short: Scalar noisy plant comparing classical CMRAC with observer-feedback CMRAC--CO.

nodes.name: Discussion of the CMRAC--CO simulation results
nodes.statement: The simulations have two distinct regions of interest, with Region 1 denoting the first 4 seconds, Region 2 denoting the 4 sec to 15 sec range. In Region 1, the adaptive system is subjected to non--zero initial conditions in the state and the reference input is zero. At $t=4$ sec, the beginning of Region 2, a filtered step input is introduced. Figures \ref{fig:ob1} and \ref{fig:ob2} illustrate the response of the CMRAC--CO adaptive system over 0 to 15 seconds, with $x_m$, $x$, and $e_m$ indicated in Figure \ref{fig:ob1}, and $u$, $\dot u$, $\theta$ and $\hat\theta$ indicated in Figure \ref{fig:ob2}. In both cases, the resulting performance is compared with the classical CMRAC system. The first point that should be noted is a satisfactory behavior in the steady-state of the CMRAC--CO adaptive controller. We note a significant difference between the responses of CMRAC--CO and CMRAC systems, which pertains to the use of noise free regressors in CMRAC--CO. An examination of $\Delta u/ \Delta t$ in Figure \ref{fig:ob2} clearly illustrates the advantage of CMRAC--CO.
nodes.statement_short: The noise-free regressor of CMRAC--CO visibly smooths $\Delta u/\Delta t$ relative to classical CMRAC.

nodes.name: Speculation on why combining direct and indirect control improves transients
nodes.statement: While the above analysis does not directly support the observed transient improvements with CMRAC, we provide a few speculations below: The free design parameter $L_i$ in the identifier is typically chosen to have eigenvalues faster than the plant that is being controlled. Therefore the identification model following error $e_i$ converges rapidly and $\hat\theta(t)$ will have smooth transients. It can be argued that the desirable transient properties of the identifier pass on to the direct component through the tuning law, and in particular $\epsilon_\theta$. The CMRAC--C differs from classical CMRAC only due to the Luenberger gain $L_m$ in the reference model. Given the contributions of Section \ref{section:perf} which show that the CRM can result in satisfactory transients without the indirect component raises the question if the added complexity of a CMRAC--C is justified. One answer to this question is in the form of the CMRAC--CO, where it is shown that one can design stable observer--based feedback in a CMRAC, allowing noise-free estimation and control.
nodes.section: Comments on CMRAC, CMRAC--C and CMRAC--CO
nodes.statement_short: A fast identifier gives smooth $\hat\theta$ whose transients pass to the direct law through $\epsilon_\theta$; CMRAC--CO justifies the added complexity.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5 (i)

nodes.statement_short: $A_m$ and $L$ commute, so the exponentials factor.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5 (ii)
nodes.statement: Let $\xi\in\Re^n$ be a normalized eigenvector of $P$. By pre-- and postmultiplying \eqref{s1:lyap} by $\xi^T$ and $\xi$, we have \ben \xi^T \bar A_m^TP \xi + \xi^T P\bar A_m \xi =- \xi^TI_{n\times n} \xi \een which reduces to \ben \lambda_i (P) \xi^T (\bar A_m +\bar A_m^T)\xi =-1. \een Expanding $\bar A_m$ we have \ben \lambda_i (P) \xi^T ( A_m + A_m^T-2 l I_{n\times n }) \xi =-1. \een Finally, using the definitions in \eqref{s1:ambound} and taking the minimum eigenvalue of $P$ we arrive at \eqref{minP} \cite{mor84}.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich the Lyapunov equation between a unit eigenvector of $P$ and take the minimum eigenvalue.
